item.title: Subsidies must reach the poor. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The World Bank’s latest findings expose a serious weakness in how subsidies and social safety-net programs are designed and delivered, with large amounts of public money failing to reach the poorest households.
This is not simply a question of inefficiency; it is a question of fairness. A system that allows wealthier households to capture a substantial share of electricity, fuel, and other subsidies while vulnerable families remain excluded is fundamentally failing in its purpose.
With poverty rising and household purchasing power under pressure, we can no longer afford to spend scarce public resources without ensuring that they produce the greatest possible benefit for those who need them.
The government must therefore undertake a serious overhaul of the system. Fragmented programs, overlapping beneficiary lists, and weak targeting must be replaced with a unified, transparent mechanism for identifying vulnerable households.
Subsidies must also become more targeted: Instead of providing broad benefits that disproportionately favour those who consume more, public funds should be directed towards households that genuinely require assistance. Cash transfers and food support should be expanded where evidence shows they can deliver greater impact, while leakages and politically influenced beneficiary selection must be eliminated.
Most importantly, reform must be measurable. The government should publish clear targets for coverage, exclusion, and leakage, and regularly report whether the poorest households are actually receiving support.
Economic hardship should not become a permanent disadvantage for the most vulnerable. Bangladesh's social protection system must stop rewarding those who are already better off and start delivering meaningful protection to those at greatest risk of being left behind.
Bangladesh cannot claim to have an effective social protection system when those who need support the most are routinely being left out.

item.title: Bangladesh’s migration future: Who bears the cost of hope?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Long before a migrant leaves Bangladesh, a family begins weighing hope against uncertainty.
How much will the journey cost? What must be borrowed or sold? How will the household manage until money starts coming home?
Behind the promise of better schooling, medical care, and a secure future lies a difficult calculation. The person leaving carries the family’s expectations; those staying behind shoulder repayments, care responsibilities, and the fear of an uncertain journey.
The experience described by a 73-year-old father captures this dilemma. A former migrant who worked in Saudi Arabia for five years, he now has two sons in Italy and another in Kuwait. His account describes families in his area arranging Tk30-40 lakh for irregular journeys to Europe through savings, loans, land sales, and mortgages.
This is a locally reported range, rather than a national estimate. Nevertheless, it shows how a migration decision can put years of accumulated assets and future income at stake.
The International Organization for Migration’s Asia–Pacific Migration Data Report 2026 gives these household pressures a wider context.
Bangladesh figures prominently as a country of migrant origin and a recipient of remittances. It also faces shifting labour markets, dangerous migration routes, and prolonged displacement. Read together, these findings raise a question: How much security does migration deliver to the people financing and undertaking it?
An estimated 8.7 million international migrants originating from Bangladesh were living abroad in 2024. Remittances are the country’s second-largest source of foreign exchange after exports, which are dominated by ready-made garments.
The report cites preliminary World Bank estimates of $33.9 billion in remittances in 2025, equivalent to around 7% of GDP. Although these calendar-year estimates remain subject to revision, they underline the importance of migrants’ earnings to the economy.
For families, those transfers mean food, treatment, school fees and the possibility of saving. But a remittance received is not necessarily money available to improve living standards. A substantial portion may go straight to lenders.
Some households finance migration by borrowing from several locally-operating microfinance institutions, alongside relatives and informal lenders. Loans may be taken in different household members’ names, creating several repayment obligations around one expected source of income: The migrant’s future earnings.
The instalments do not necessarily wait for that income to arrive. A migrant may still be travelling, stranded in transit, or waiting for work when repayments begin. Some spend prolonged periods in broker-controlled accommodation, including spaces sometimes described as “game rooms,” awaiting onward movement.
Conditions vary, but uncertain departures, additional payment demands, and limited communication can leave families with little control over events.
Even arrival does not guarantee financial relief. Workers need dependable employment, regular wages, and enough income after living expenses to send money home. Until then, relatives must cover installments from existing earnings, savings, or further borrowing. Spending on healthcare, schooling and food may be squeezed. Assets intended to secure the family’s future may be sold to meet its immediate obligations.
Financial pressure is accompanied by emotional strain. A delayed telephone call can provoke fears about detention, exploitation, or a dangerous crossing. Migrants may feel compelled to continue because their families have invested heavily.
Relatives may agree to further payments because refusing seems to endanger the traveller or sacrifice everything already spent. These pressures deserve attention in migration services.
The father’s account helps explain why warnings alone may fail. Young people compare uncertain local livelihoods with the houses, land, and businesses acquired by successful migrants. Stories of success circulate through relatives, neighbours, and social media. Failed journeys and lingering debts can be less visible.
Families are making decisions within this social landscape. Their willingness to accept danger should not be mistaken for indifference to it. When local opportunities appear inadequate and regular pathways remain difficult to access, a hazardous offer can become painfully persuasive. Meaningful choice requires credible alternatives.
The IOM report shows how vulnerable existing opportunities are to changes abroad. Registered overseas labour outflows reached approximately 1.13 million in 2025, below the 2023 peak. Departures to Malaysia fell to 3,451, around 99% below 2023 levels. Outflows to the United Arab Emirates declined by 70% from 2024, while only 671 departures to Oman were recorded. Growth in other destinations partly offset these contractions.
For prospective workers, such changes can leave paid-for plans suspended. September reporting that Malaysia-bound workers were awaiting clarity about costs, medical tests, and departure dates illustrates the consequences.
Reopening a labour market matters only when workers can access verified jobs through transparent procedures and obtain remedies when recruitment fails.
Bangladesh needs firmer accountability throughout the recruitment chain. Workers should receive understandable contracts, itemized charges, receipts, and reliable employer verification. Agencies must answer for intermediaries acting on their behalf. Complaints should produce timely investigations, with refunds or compensation where justified.
A phased transition towards employer-paid recruitment should be a diplomatic priority. Meanwhile, lenders need to assess a household’s combined obligations rather than each loan separately. Financing verified overseas employment should allow repayment arrangements that reflect the time required to begin earning. Debt counselling, appropriate restructuring and psychosocial support should be available when recruitment fails or workers experience exploitation.
The European-route figures make these reforms urgent. Bangladeshis accounted for 24,318 recorded irregular arrivals from Asia to Europe in 2025, approximately 52% of that regional total. They represented three quarters of Asian arrivals on the Central Mediterranean route. Recorded Bangladeshi arrivals on the Eastern Mediterranean route rose from 1,133 in 2024 to 3,831 in 2025.
The report describes sea journeys from Libya towards Italy and, increasingly, from eastern Libya to Crete and Gavdos in Greece. It also records Bangladeshi transit movements through the Western Balkans. Journeys can combine regular travel to transit countries with irregular onward crossings. Each interruption can prolong family anxiety while loan obligations continue.
Bangladesh’s diplomacy must address conditions along these journeys. Rescue, legal assistance, family contact, and wage recovery should receive sustained attention. People travelling through irregular channels must receive humane treatment and protection. Return arrangements should consider individual circumstances, with reintegration support addressing health, debt, and employment.
Training also needs a clearer connection to employment. A September 28 consultation reported in The Daily Star highlighted weak links between skills programs and jobs, alongside difficulties securing recognition of qualifications abroad. Training should follow verified demand and include practical competence and language preparation. Placement, earnings, and job retention should determine whether it works.
Migration policy must also account for those who remain at home. Spouses and grandparents often take on additional care responsibilities. Children’s learning and older people’s well-being deserve support. Women, who represented only 6% of recorded labour outflows in 2025, need affordable training, safe accommodation, and effective protection against harassment and exploitation.
Displacement adds another layer of insecurity. IOM’s nationwide assessment with the government estimated 4.96 million disaster-related internally displaced people as of October 2025. Around 63% had been displaced before April 2020. This enduring population is distinct from the 105,000 new disaster-related displacement events recorded in 2025.
Housing, education, healthcare, and livelihood assistance must address that duration. Climate diplomacy should seek adaptation and loss-and-damage financing that supports communities’ choices about remaining, relocating, or rebuilding.
Bangladesh should measure migration’s success through recruitment costs, household debt, wage recovery, and family well-being alongside remittance receipts. Migrants and their families must help shape that assessment.
A family borrowing to finance migration is investing in hope. Public institutions and international partnerships should help ensure that the hope survives the journey and becomes security when earnings finally come home.
Iqbal Ehsan is a development professional and researcher. Email: ehsan656@gmail.com .

item.title: WTO hikes global trade growth forecast, names Pakistan among nations gaining from disruptions amid ME conflict. [ dawn ]
item.description:
ISLAMABAD: The World Trade Organisation on Thursday sharply raised its global trade growth forecast for 2026 — with merchandise trade riding the AI boom — and concluded that some nations, including Pakistan, were actually benefiting from trade disruptions amid the ongoing Middle East conflict in some ways.

In its Global Trade Outlook Update 2026, the Geneva-based global trade watchdog said its economists had upgraded their forecasts for global merchandise trade volume growth to 3.9 per cent for 2026 and 4.1pc for 2027 — up from previous estimates of 1.9pc and 2.6pc, respectively, projected at the start of the US-Iran conflict in March.

The report said that despite the conflict, the global economy had remained resilient, reflecting a stronger-than-expected surge in AI-related capital investment and increased supplies of fuels and fertilisers from countries outside the Middle East.

While several countries faced fuel transport disruptions because of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, the redistribution of traffic was creating opportunities for various other economies, it said.

“For example, Pakistan’s exports of sea freight transport services rose by 73pc year-on-year in the first half of 2026, as its transport operators benefited from increased traffic,” the WTO said.

Vessel calls at major container terminals in Karachi were still 14pc higher year-on-year in July, it added.

Exports by the United States to the European Union continued to expand while exports to Asia and the Pacific decreased by 2pc in the second quarter.

At the same time, computer services exports by several smaller and emerging players expanded rapidly. In the second quarter, computer services exports from Malaysia rose by 34pc, those from Pakistan by 23pc and by 13pc in Brazil.

The WTO also noted that the rerouting of vessels and containers towards alternative ports and trans-shipment hubs had put pressure on capacity in South Asia, translating into higher charges. In July, the Mediterranean Shipping Company (MSC) introduced a congestion surcharge of $500 per container on shipments from Northern Europe to India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

“Longer waiting and transit times are increasing costs for carriers and traders, some of which may ultimately be passed on to consumers,” it said.

Stronger-than-expected growth reflects opposing forces

The report revised the forecast for commercial services trade volume growth in 2026 down to 3.3pc from the previous 4.8pc, as the conflict in the Middle East has depressed travel and tourism in the region and raised fuel input costs worldwide.

In 2027, growth rates in volume terms for merchandise and commercial services trade were expected to rise to 4.1pc and 6.4pc, respectively, but this outcome depended on a timely resolution of the Middle East conflict, according to the WTO.

Based on these projections, the volume of global goods and services trade was expected to grow by approximately 3.7pc in 2026 and 4.7pc in 2027, the organisation forecast.

The stronger-than-expected growth in merchandise trade reflects two opposing forces, according to the watchdog. On the one hand, the push from AI-related investment has increased demand for AI-enabling goods, which accounted for 47pc of global merchandise trade growth in value terms in the first half of 2026. On the other hand, reduced shipments of oil, natural gas and fertilisers have weighed on merchandise trade; for the ongoing year to date, the former has outweighed the latter, the WTO said.

It noted that while high commodity prices may persist as a result of bottlenecks constraining the flows of fuels and fertilisers, continued AI investment and the broader digitisation of the global economy were expected to keep merchandise trade growth above the rate of global GDP growth in 2027.

“AI investment and the Middle East conflict are also affecting the services trade outlook, but to different degrees. AI is lifting trade in computer and financial services. However, the impact of the conflict in the Middle East is prevailing in traditional services such as transport, tourism and construction,” it said.

Conversely, services trade growth is expected to remain below trend this year before rebounding in 2027. Asia and North America are expected to see their contributions decline, while those of Europe are expected to remain broadly stable, putting the region on track to account for over half of the growth in export services this year.

Meanwhile, the rest of the world was expected to make a negative contribution, dragged down by a large contraction in the Middle East, the report added. All services sub-sectors are expected to see growth below the March baseline forecast.

However, it noted that the trade forecast remains subject to several significant risks.

“The current wedge between crude oil and refined oil prices is weighing on trade growth by eroding households’ purchasing power. A slowdown or reversal of AI investment spending could also have a significant impact on trade given its high import content,” it said.

Turning to trade statistics in value terms, the WTO said the current US dollar value of world merchandise trade had risen considerably faster than volume in the first half of 2026, up 15pc year-on-year compared to 3.5pc growth in volume terms.

“This marks one of the largest gaps between the value and volume of trade growth in recent years, reflecting higher prices for fuels and electronic components for data centres,” it said.

It noted that trade continued to show “some alignment with geopolitical considerations”, although it pointed out that the gap between intra-bloc and inter-bloc trade had narrowed through 2025 and into 2026, suggesting that “the broader pattern of bloc-based fragmentation has not continued to intensify”.

US-China trade decoupling had, however, accelerated since 2025 and was now the main driver of the bloc divergence, it added.

item.title: Cushioning the fall: The urgent need to protect Bangladesh’s new poor. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is navigating a deeply troubling period in its national life. Poverty is on the rise, yet neither the chronically poor nor the newly poor are being provided with adequate economic cushions to absorb the shocks.
Worse, nearly 62 million people live just above the poverty line -- just one shock away from falling back into destitution.
Last Tuesday, I read with rapt attention two reports that arrived in my mailbox, both released from Washington, DC. By sheer coincidence, both focused on a critical issue: Ensuring that the social safety net benefits promised by the government actually reach the people who need them most.
The World Bank, in its flagship Bangladesh Development Update , and the food policy think tank IFPRI, in its policy note Modernizing Bangladesh's Social Protection System , highlighted how Bangladesh’s fragmented social safety net programs fail to adequately support their intended beneficiaries -- the poorest of the poor.
At a time when the number of Bangladeshis living below the poverty line is rising for the fourth consecutive year in 2026, it is deeply worrying that a substantial portion of the budget allocated for the poor is ending up in the hands of the non-poor.
The poor are already under severe pressure from widespread joblessness, factory closures, persistent high inflation, and a rising cost of living driven by successive energy price hikes.
The share of the ultra-poor has nearly doubled, from 5.9% in 2022 to a projected 10.1% this year, while the overall poverty rate is projected to rise from 18.7% to 22.5% over the same four-year period.
In total, an estimated eight million people have slipped into poverty between 2022 and 2026, with more than two million joining their ranks in the past year alone.
The core challenge facing Bangladesh’s social protection system is increasingly one of efficiency and coherence rather than aggregate spending. In FY27, the government allocated Tk1.44 trillion to social protection, equivalent to 2.1% of GDP. Yet actual pro-poor spending remains severely limited.
Like the World Bank report, the IFPRI authors Akhter U Ahmed and Md Sadat Anowar also point out, the system is plagued by extreme fragmentation and structural inefficiencies:
Institutional fragmentation: The government administers 90 social protection programs across 25 ministries, resulting in separate eligibility rules, duplicate beneficiary lists, serious coordination challenges, and high transaction costs.
Misallocated funds: Government employee pensions and agricultural subsidies alone account for about 43% of the total social protection budget. The pension program for retired government employees alone accounts for 29% of total spending.
Weak poverty targeting: The 48 programs officially classified as “pro-poor” receive only about 39% of the social protection budget. Moreover, nearly 48% of this pro-poor allocation is concentrated in just four flagship transfers: Family Card, Old Age Allowance, Widow and Destitute Women Allowance, and Disability Allowance.
Highly uneven distribution: The five largest programs absorb about 67% of the budget but reach only 5.5% of beneficiaries. This leaves the remaining programs severely underfunded, resulting in negligible benefits and limited coverage for those who need support the most.
The consequences of these systemic gaps are stark. While the share of households reporting receipt of assistance rose from 24.6% in 2010 to 37.6% in recent years, half of the poorest households remain entirely outside the reach of any safety net.
Conversely, current transfers benefit 31% of people in the richest income quintile.
Alarmingly, the share of total benefits reaching the bottom 40% of the population fell from 51% in 2016 to about 44% in 2022. Meanwhile, broad-based energy and fertilizer subsidies provide significant financial assistance but disproportionately benefit better-off households.
There is a pressing need to improve targeting, increase benefit amounts, expand urban coverage, and scale up successful programs while phasing out inefficient ones so that the effectiveness of the social protection system in uplifting the poor is enhanced.
By improving targeting and reducing benefit leakage, social protection coverage for poor households can be expanded even within the current budget.
It is high time for Bangladesh to review its entire social protection system. The government must redesign and realign these programs to ensure that benefits are substantial, integrated, and strictly targeted towards the population segments that need those most to survive the current wave of economic shocks.
Stronger coordination, interoperable delivery systems, and a shift away from untargeted subsidies are urgently needed to create a coherent social protection architecture.
If we fail to undertake this structural overhaul, massive budgetary allocations will continue to flow into the wrong hands. Meanwhile, the most vulnerable citizens will find it increasingly difficult to cope with skyrocketing inflation, a slowing economy, and pervasive unemployment.
Bangladesh cannot afford support systems that absorb substantial public resources without effectively protecting those most affected by economic shocks. The government must act now to strengthen and leverage its social protection framework so that it can respond effectively to this period of heightened economic stress and external uncertainty.
Reaz Ahmad is Editor, Dhaka Tribune.

item.title: No exit: Why Bangladesh's cities keep burning. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
For the last fifteen years, buildings have been catching fire for the same reasons, with the same promises following each tragedy. If resilience truly starts at home, then home, in Bangladesh's cities, is precisely where it keeps failing.
Every October 13 , the world observes the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction. This year's theme, "Resilience starts at home," is meant to be read gently, as a call to prepare our households for disasters. In urban Bangladesh, it reads more like a warning.
A city that keeps reliving the same night
The roll call is long and familiar. From the Nimtoli chemical warehouse fire in 2010, which killed at least 124 people, to the Tazreen factory fire in 2012, the Bailey Road restaurant fire in 2024 and the Korail fire in 2025, Bangladesh's cities have repeatedly witnessed preventable loss of life and homes.
Across such incidents, well over 400 people have died. Almost none of the resulting court cases have reached a verdict.
The details differ, but the pattern does not: the conditions that allow a fire to become a disaster are often present long before the first flame.
The disaster is often built before the fire starts
Faulty electrical wiring and overloaded circuits are among the most common triggers. Gas cylinders used in homes, restaurants and vehicles can turn routine activities into deadly emergencies. Chemical warehouses and flammable stock are routinely stored in buildings never designed to contain them, turning a fire into an inferno within minutes.
Factories and high-rise commercial buildings with inadequate or locked emergency exits become death traps when smoke fills a corridor. Restaurants have proliferated on upper floors of buildings not designed for such use, sometimes obstructing escape routes. In informal settlements, tightly packed housing, exposed wiring and narrow lanes can allow a single spark to spread across an entire neighbourhood.
The problem, then, is not simply fire. Risk is built into the way buildings are designed, approved, occupied and maintained.
Rules on paper, risk in practice
Bangladesh is not short of regulation. The Bangladesh National Building Code, mandatory since 2006 and updated in 2020, sets out fire-resistant design, mandatory exits, hydrants, sprinklers and detection systems, and any building must secure fire safety clearance from the Fire Service and Civil Defence before RAJUK approves its design.
The gap is not in the law; it is in its application. A parliamentary disclosure put the share of Dhaka buildings violating the code at around 66 per cent. A RAJUK survey of over 200,000 structures found roughly two-thirds defective, risky or uninhabitable, while separate data found nine in ten surveyed buildings deviated from their approved designs. Too often, a design approved on paper is altered or repurposed in practice, without effective follow-up.
From certificates to inspections that bite
Closing this gap does not require new laws so much as the will to enforce existing ones. Building and fire approvals need to be digitised and linked, so a change of use or an expired licence is visible to regulators automatically rather than discovered after a tragedy.
Fire clearance should not be a one-time certificate issued at construction; it needs to be a recurring inspection, with real penalties, including sealing premises, for buildings that let it lapse. The Bangladesh Building Regulatory Authority envisaged under the BNBC 2020 should be operationalised with a clear mandate for consistent enforcement. RAJUK, city corporations and the Fire Service need enough trained inspectors to visit the hundreds of thousands of buildings under their jurisdiction. And court cases following major fires need to reach a verdict.
Six policy fixes we cannot keep postponing
Planners, engineers, lawyers and fire-safety experts have converged on broadly the same list of reforms after each tragedy; what has been missing is follow-through.
First , establish a dedicated Building Regulatory Authority to implement the Building Code consistently, instead of leaving it split across RAJUK, city corporations and the Fire Service with no single body accountable.
Second , harmoni z e the Fire Prevention and Extinction Act 2003 with the Building Code, so the two frameworks set the same standard.
Third , publish a tiered public registry of high- and moderate-risk buildings, so tenants and regulators know which structures need urgent attention before they burn.
Fourth , require every building to display an annually renewable occupancy and fire safety certificate at its entrance.
Fifth , make hospital, industrial and commercial fire protocols mandatory: functioning lifts, unlocked and clearly marked exits, refuge floors and regular evacuation drills.
Sixth , back all of this with real investment in the Fire Service's staffing and equipment, alongside a coordinated national occupational safety framework of the kind the International Labour Organization has urged Bangladesh to adopt since the Bailey Road incident.
Resilience starts at home, or it does not start at all
Every fire on this list was, in hindsight, foreseeable: a blocked exit, a warehouse in the wrong place, a licence never renewed. Resilience starting at home means exactly that literal thing here -- a safe electrical line, a clear staircase, a landlord who does not store chemicals beneath a family's bedroom.
Government agencies can write codes and NGOs can rebuild what fire destroys, but neither can retrofit safety into a building after the fact. Bangladesh's cities do not lack rules; they lack the follow-through to make those rules real, in every home, before the next spark catches.
Khondoker Golam Tawhid is the Programme Head of the Disaster Risk Management Programme at BRAC .

Fixing our banking sector. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Reports that the International Monetary Fund will likely press for strict, time-bound deadlines to fix weak banks and reduce the astronomical non-performing loans (NPLs) we have racked up should serve as a wake-up call for our leaders.
Despite dreams of self-sufficiency, the reality we must contend with is that, at present, our economic delegations are preparing to negotiate a fresh financial package with international lenders.
To that end, it is also abundantly clear that if we are to continue to receive the financial assistance our economy needs, Bangladesh can no longer afford half-measures in reforming what can safely be referred to as its crippled banking sector.
Decades of political patronage, reckless default cultures, and opaque loan write-offs have brought our financial architecture to the brink. As such, we simply no longer have the option to treat bank reform as an optional administrative exercise.
The rot in our financial system is neither hidden nor new. For years, massive amounts of liquidity have been siphoned off through fraud, insider lending, and willful defaults, leaving state-owned and private commercial banks saddled with staggering piles of debt.
It goes without saying that a banking sector choking on defaulted loans cannot be of help to the economy, thereby stunting our growth and deepening the broader fiscal crisis.
While no nation likes external pressure, we would do well to not view it as an infringement on sovereignty, but rather as a catalyst for accountability.
Financial stability is the backbone of national security and economic survival, and it is a shame that Bangladesh has not experienced it for some time now, if ever.
If setting strict deadlines is what is needed to cleanse our balance sheets and end the culture of loan default, then so be it. We must do what we can to restore public trust and build a modern, transparent banking system.

item.title: Controlling dengue requires a national strategy rooted in One Health. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
Dengue in Bangladesh is no longer a temporary or seasonal health inconvenience; it has evolved into a persistent, multi-faceted public health crisis and a heavy burden on the national economy.
According to the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) dengue dashboard, over 107,000 individuals have been hospitalized, and more than 331 deaths have been officially documented as of October 15, 2026. With approximately 2,000 new patients admitted daily, the strain on the healthcare system is overwhelming.
Major tertiary hospitals in Dhaka and urban hubs are facing severe shortages of hospital beds and intensive care unit (ICU) capacities. Relatives face frantic scrambles for blood platelets, revealing the systemic fragility of urban medical infrastructure.
These alarming conditions highlight a critical truth: Reactive clinical management after people fall ill, paired with ad-hoc vector control drives, cannot control the transmission chain.
What Bangladesh urgently requires is a year-round, evidence-based preventive policy anchored in a coordinated national framework.
The uninterrupted spread of dengue is deeply intertwined with climate change, unplanned rapid urbanization, chronic waterlogging, and inadequate municipal waste management.
Global environmental and epidemiological research demonstrates that climate volatility, characterized by rising mean temperatures, erratic unseasonal precipitation, and elevated atmospheric humidity, dramatically accelerates the breeding cycles and vector efficiency of Aedes mosquitoes.
Under higher ambient temperatures, the duration required for the dengue virus to replicate inside the mosquito and reach its salivary glands, is significantly shortened. Consequently, an infected female Aedes mosquito becomes capable of transmitting the pathogen to human hosts much faster and more frequently within its lifespan.
Concurrently, urban environments proliferate with artificial micro-habitats. Construction sites, poorly designed drainage infrastructure, discarded single-use plastics, and poorly maintained rooftop gardens collect stagnant water, offering ideal breeding conditions.
Relying exclusively on hospital-centred curative care to address what is inherently an environmental and eco-climatic phenomenon is inherently flawed.
For decades, vector control efforts in Bangladesh have remained stubbornly reactive. Intervention plans are typically mobilized only after hospital admissions surge to crisis levels, taking the form of temporary fogging drives or hospital bed expansions.
Yet, such reactive measures fail to answer fundamental operational questions:
Indiscriminate fogging without routine entomological monitoring wastes municipal resources and damages urban ecosystems, killing beneficial non-target insects while accelerating insecticide resistance in Aedes vectors.
Transitioning from reactive fogging to sustainable vector management demands source reduction, routine larvicidal suppression, systematic waste removal, and targeted bio-control methods.
In this complex landscape, the 'One Health' framework offers the most viable path forward. One Health is an integrated, unifying approach that recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human health, animal health, and the shared environment.
While dengue is not directly transmitted from animals to humans, it is a vector-borne viral disease reliant on the interaction between human hosts, viral pathogens, mosquito vectors, and ambient environmental conditions.
Applying One Health to dengue control means treating vector ecology, climatic dynamics, human mobility, and urban sanitation as a single interconnected ecosystem.
It breaks down traditional administrative silos, bringing together public health physicians, specialists, medical entomologists, environmental scientists, climate researchers, urban planners, and municipal engineers onto a unified operational platform.
The government recently formed a high-level special taskforce comprising representatives across various ministries and authorities to oversee mosquito-borne disease management, a commendable administrative step.
However, to translate policy into measurable health outcomes, this taskforce must move beyond administrative governance and actively embed the One Health framework into its operational core, with entomologists, climate specialists, and One Health practitioners needing to hold direct scientific advisory roles.
Crucially, Bangladesh needs a predictive national early warning and surveillance system that synthesizes real-time meteorological forecasts, rainfall patterns, vector density indices, larval mapping, and clinical hospitalization data.
Analyzing these spatial data streams will allow authorities to forecast outbreak clusters weeks before human cases spike, shifting intervention efforts from reactive crisis management to pre-emptive prevention.
Academic institutions and research centres must also be integrated into local intervention trials to evaluate the efficacy of eco-friendly larvicides and biological vector suppression tools tailored to micro-climatic zones.
Community participation remains vital to sustaining these interventions. Public awareness campaigns must empower citizens to inspect their surroundings, eliminate standing water, dispose of water-retaining trash, and neutralize mosquito breeding sites around homes.
However, civic responsibility must not serve as an excuse for institutional inaction. Local municipal authorities bear the primary obligation to ensure reliable solid waste collection, maintain open drainage canals, prevent waterlogging, and enforce environmental compliance across urban construction projects.
Controlling dengue demands a departure from fragmented, seasonal measures in favour of a long-term, science-driven, and accountable national strategy.
Clinical preparedness must be balanced with environmental management, integrated surveillance, and robust inter-ministerial coordination.
Ultimately, the success of national dengue control must not be measured by how many hospital beds are arranged to treat the sick, but by how many infections are prevented, how many vector breeding sites are permanently eliminated, and how many lives are protected.
Without a structural transition to a One Health paradigm, Bangladesh will remain trapped in a recurring cycle of preventable loss of life and severe economic strain year after year.
Professor Dr KBM Saiful Islam is the former Dean of the Faculty of Animal Science & Veterinary Medicine and former Chairman of the Department of Medicine & Public Health at Sher‑e‑Bangla Agricultural University. He previously served as a member of the National Coordination Committee of One Health Bangladesh.

Bangladesh is battling measles. It's a 'real warning' to other nations. [ dawn ]
item.description:
Bangladesh is battling to contain the world’s worst measles outbreak, a crisis exacerbated by weak data, inadequate outreach and vaccination gaps that experts say offers a warning to other nations about the deadly risk of falling immunisation rates.

Bangladesh, whose routine vaccination programme faltered in 2025, reported 202,000 suspected measles cases – 22,000 of them laboratory-confirmed – since the start of the outbreak in mid-March to October 9, the World Health Organisation said. That’s more suspected cases than any other country this year.

So far, 1,147 people have died of the highly contagious disease, with 94 per cent of reported deaths among children under five years old, the WHO said.

Bangladesh’s experience shows the challenge of containing an outbreak when vaccination coverage falls below 95pc, a level the WHO says is needed to prevent outbreaks. Bangladesh almost achieved that in recent years but in 2025 coverage dropped.

A Reuters review of WHO documents, alongside interviews with more than a dozen scientists, health workers and officials, shows Bangladesh was also hampered in its emergency response by data that left out millions of children, shortcomings in preparation and a failure to reach enough parents.

“This is a real warning to every country,” said Mark Jit, a WHO vaccine adviser and professor at the School of Global Public Health at New York University.

Preventing an outbreak through vaccinations was easier, cheaper and safer than responding to an emergency, he said.

“The response will stop the outbreak eventually, but in the meantime, many will have had measles, and some will have died,” he said.

Ziauddin Hyder, special assistant on health affairs to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, told Reuters in September the government was doing everything it could to end the outbreak. The government did not respond to further questions sent in October for this article.

‘They came only after i Buried my son’

In the northeast Sylhet region, one of the worst-hit areas in the nation of 178 million people, two-year-old Arman Hossain died unvaccinated in July, 24 hours after admission to hospital for treatment paid for by selling the family’s three-wheeled auto rickshaw. His unvaccinated four-year-old sister survived.

His father Amin Mia, 26, said no health workers came to their remote village in Sylhet to offer vaccinations in time. “They came only after I buried my son,” he said.

Measles usually kills two or three people in every 1,000 cases, the WHO says, but the disease can be more deadly in poorer nations because of factors such as malnutrition.

In the town of Chhatak, also in the Sylhet region, the daughter of 30-year-old carpenter Humayun Rashid died unvaccinated in June aged nine months. Labiba Akter could have received an inoculation in April when an emergency programme lowered the vaccination age to six months from nine.

“No health worker came to tell us,” her father said.

In a report published in July this year, WHO and UNICEF estimated first-dose coverage in 2025 had fallen to 90pc, while second-dose coverage was 86pc, several percentage points below the 95pc needed for herd immunity.

The report also raised questions about the quality of official data on vaccinations for measles and other diseases for the years 2023 to 2025.

It said preliminary figures sometimes showed numbers of those inoculated exceeded 100pc of those targeted, indicating mistakes in counting doses or target numbers.

item.description:
Bangladesh seeks answers after Saudi Arabia executes two of its citizens without notice

Submitted by Areeb Ullah on Mon, 10/19/2026 - 12:59
Dhaka said it was not informed by Saudi Arabia that it had executed the pair arrested in Mecca for 'indecent acts'
Bangladeshi workers sitting outside an airport after flights to Saudi Arabia were cancelled following a series of Houthi attacks in October (AFP/Piyas Biswas)
Off

Bangladesh is seeking answers on why Saudi Arabia executed two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca without telling Dhaka.

Last week, Saudi Arabia executed a male and a female Bangladeshi national after they were convicted of committing “indecent acts” inside a mosque.

Riyadh did not provide further details on the acts the two Bangladeshi nationals allegedly committed or whether they had legal representation in the Gulf kingdom, according to local media reports.

Reacting to the incident, Bangladesh’s minister for foreign affairs, Humaiun Kobir, told reporters that he was “very disappointed” by the lack of communication and that Dhaka was seeking an explanation on why they were executed and not informed beforehand about the execution.

“We have sought an explanation from our friendly bilateral partner to look into the matter and know why the gap in information sharing and exchanges happened here. We are in discussions," he told reporters at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday.

Earlier, the Bangladeshi foreign ministry said that it was waiting for a copy of the full verdict and the circumstances that led to the execution.

The official added that the two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh but did not indicate that they had planned to execute them.

Last week, Saudi Arabia’s Supreme Court overturned the death sentence of a Sri Lankan national after he allegedly insulted Islam and the Prophet Muhammad.

Sri Lanka’s Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra confirmed that Riyadh had overturned the death sentence of Anojan Sivarasa.

The 27-year-old remains imprisoned after he was sentenced to five years in prison and fined three million Saudi Riyals ($800,000).

The court handed down the sentence amid intense criticism of Riyadh's legal system.

Saudi Arabia relies on interpretations of Islamic law, alongside cybercrime and counterterror legislation, to target online expression under the guise of protecting "public morals".

This has resulted in a surge of decades-long prison terms for social media users and an increased use of capital punishment.

At least 175 people have been executed so far this year, the majority of whom are foreign nationals.

We cannot ignore our real wage crisis. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
We should be deeply concerned by the fact that inflation has outpaced wage growth for 56 consecutive months, as per reports from the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS).
This streak of stagnant earnings falling behind soaring commodity prices can no longer be seen as a temporary metric of market friction and must be called what it is, and what it has been for some time - a full-blown livelihood crisis eroding the very fabric of our working and middle classes.
What must be recognized is the human toll behind these metrics, which is extremely stark. National survey data from BBS shows that to bridge the current shortfall, a staggering 47.42% of Bangladeshi households - and over 51% in rural areas - are needing to take on high-interest informal debt simply to put food on the table.
When citizens are forced to borrow money not to build assets, but to cover daily meals and basic utilities, we can conclude that the state’s socio-economic safety net has effectively failed. Given that this has been ongoing for almost five years now, this failure must be attributed to every single administration we have had during this time period.
In the absence of enforceable wage protections and automatic inflation-adjusted pay revisions, workers and employees alike are forced to absorb the full, brutal impact of macroeconomic shocks while corporate margins and profits remain shielded.
We cannot have a government that continues to remain a passive spectator to this erosion of basic purchasing power. Economic progress that enriches a privileged few while draining the savings of the working majority is morally indefensible, structurally unsustainable, and not the kind of progress any nation should be proud of.
The state must act now to restore real wages before our economic squeeze fractures our society beyond repair.

item.title: Why do foreign governments and lenders still want to invest in Bangladesh?. [ dhakatribune ]
item.description:
The IMF's October World Economic Outlook forecasts 3.2% growth for Bangladesh in FY27, down from 4.3% in April, with average inflation rising to 10.9%.
A week earlier, the World Bank cut its own forecast to 3.4% and said the weakness would persist through FY28, while it expects South Asia to grow at 6.9%.
If the IMF is right, this will be the slowest growth since FY1988-89, and place Bangladesh last among the seven South Asian economies in its table.
India is projected to grow at more than twice Bangladesh's rate. Sri Lanka, which defaulted on its external debt in 2022, is projected to grow faster than Bangladesh this year, as are Pakistan and Nepal. The medium-term outlook is weaker still, as the IMF projects Bangladesh's growth to fall to 2.2% in FY28 (Figure 1).
Yet over the same months, despite the grim forecasts for growth, the news from Dhaka has been of foreign governments and multilateral lenders showing strong interest in deepening their investments in Bangladesh.
The joint declaration of Bangladesh and China in June committed the two governments to modernize Mongla Port, develop a Chinese economic and industrial zone in Chittagong, and speed up the feasibility study for the Teesta project. In August, the Chinese ambassador said these projects could attract around 30 Chinese companies investing about $500 million.
Japan signed an Economic Partnership Agreement with Bangladesh in February and an emergency support loan for economic resilience and energy supply in June. Its plans now go further, as senior Japanese diplomats told The Hindu last week that Tokyo wants to build an industrial value chain around the JICA-financed deep-sea port at Matarbari, linking India's seven northeastern states, Nepal, Bhutan, and Myanmar to the Bay of Bengal. Prime Minister Tarique Rahman is expected in Tokyo at the end of October to seek Japanese financing for a Matarbari industrial, port, and commercial hub for 2026-2031.
On October 13, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation met the PM, who welcomed Dutch interest in the Teesta feasibility study. A senior US State Department adviser has said Bangladesh could soon become eligible for financing from the US international development finance corporation. South Korea expects its trade agreement with Bangladesh, still awaiting signature, to raise Korean investment.
The multilateral lenders show the same interest. Bangladesh is the largest borrower from the World Bank's International Development Association, with an exposure of $22.7bn as of March 2026. The ADB committed$2.685bn to Bangladesh in FY26. The relationship with the IMF is also intact.
The finance minister's statement on October 4 that he had cancelled the IMF program was read as an exit. In fact, the IMF confirmed in June that Bangladesh had applied for a new program, and in July, the finance minister said the two sides had agreed on its broad framework.
Little more than a week after his statement, the minister sought the support of the IMF and the World Bank in Bangkok. The government is leaving the program it inherited to negotiate new conditions. It is not leaving the fund.
Why would these governments and lenders want to invest in an economy that is not poised to perform?
My answer is that a market of more than 170 million people does not shrink when its growth rate does. That gives Bangladesh a bargaining position few countries with such a forecast have. The evidence from other countries supports four reasons.
Firstly , investors follow the size of a market more than its growth rate. In 2016, in the middle of a deep recession, Brazil still received about $78.9bn of foreign direct investment, nearly half of the inflows to Latin America.
The proposals for Bangladesh follow the same logic. The Invest Bangladesh pipeline is led by renewable energy and information technology, and the Chinese proposals include the Dhaka-Chittagong highway and waste-to-energy plants. These serve the domestic market.
By my own arithmetic, even 3.2% growth on an economy of about $470bn adds around $15bn of output in a year.
Secondly , governments compete for influence in large and well-placed countries. In 2015, Indonesia awarded the Jakarta-Bandung high-speed rail to China over Japan after China agreed to build it without an Indonesian government guarantee, while Japan had offered a loan at 0.1% interest.
Bangladesh sits in the same contest, as China, Japan, the Netherlands, and the United States all seek a role in its ports, rivers, and energy.
China and the Netherlands have both offered support on the Teesta feasibility study. Japan's answer is Matarbari, and its diplomats cite the Southern Economic Corridor linking Thailand, Cambodia, and Vietnam as the model.
Thirdly , supply chains are moving out of China. Vietnam drew a record $25.35bn in foreign direct investment in 2024 as manufacturers diversified, helped by its trade agreements and lower labour costs.
The agreement with Japan, China's zero-tariff treatment of Bangladeshi goods, and the planned agreement with South Korea give Bangladesh a similar platform.
Fourthly , multilateral lenders do not walk away from large borrowers. In 2024, Egypt secured an IMF program of $8 billion, a World Bank package of $6 billion and EU support of €7.4bn. In Nigeria, where I also work, the World Bank approved about $9.35bn between June 2023 and May 2026, after the government removed the petrol subsidy and unified the exchange rate. In my reading, the financing in both countries was tied to reform.
However, most of this interest is still a promise, not an investment.
Ashik Chowdhury, who now chairs Invest Bangladesh, said in June that the Chinese company’s proposals had not been verified. Of the $1.3bn pipeline his agency reported in September, only a little over $400m had reached the decision or implementation stage.
UNCTAD puts total foreign direct investment into Bangladesh in 2025 at $1.8bn, and the World Bank's own commitment fell to $820m in FY26, its lowest. Interest lapses if the government does not convert it.
To secure these investments, the Ministry of Finance should conclude the new IMF program quickly, as finance ministry officials themselves describe an active program as a seal of approval that unlocks other financing.
In return, the government should accept the IMF’s conditions on raising tax revenue. Bangladesh collects only 8.3% of GDP in tax, among the lowest ratios in the world. The IMF mission discussed measures to raise that ratio as early as July, and no lender will drop the condition.
Each G2G partnership also needs a single owner in government and a published timetable, as the published accounts of the declaration with China give no cost or date for Mongla, Chittagong, or Teesta.
Invest Bangladesh should publish a quarterly tracker of every proposal and its stage. The government should also hold to the five-year tax outlook it presented to Chinese investors.
Size is the reason an economy like Bangladesh always has room to turn around. The governments and lenders now showing interest are betting on the market, not on this year's growth rate.
However, the turnaround will not happen unless the government removes the constraints the World Bank has named: Gas and electricity shortages that disrupt industry, non-performing loans that reached 33.2% in June, and weak revenue collection.
The Matarbari plan also depends on relations with India, as the Maitri Bridge over the Feni river, the link to Tripura, is not operating.
The government will keep its bargaining position only if it turns this interest into signed investment before the investors look elsewhere.
Md Rubaiyath Sarwar is Managing Director of Innovision Consulting and Trustee at Panam Institute, an Economic Think-Tank .
